item.title: Indonesian miners scramble for clarity as Prabowo seeks greater state share
item.description: Miners in Indonesia, the world’s biggest exporter of thermal coal, nickel and tin, are scrambling to decipher President Prabowo Subianto’s call for the st
item.dc:creator: Mining.com
item.content:encoded: Miners in Indonesia, the world’s biggest exporter of thermal coal, nickel and tin, are scrambling to decipher President Prabowo Subianto’s call for the state to secure greater benefits from mining operations, warning that the uncertainty could deter investment in the resource-rich nation. The comments add to concerns among investors over policy uncertainty in Southeast Asia’s largest economy – home to the world’s largest gold mine and the biggest known nickel reserves – which has already been rattled by warnings from international credit ratings agencies and the prospect of MSCI excluding the country from its stock market indexes. Indonesia’s energy stock index .JKENERGY, which includes shares of coal miners, has dropped 4.1% since Prabowo’s weekend comments – while the basic materials stock index .JKBASIC, which covers miners of other minerals, has lost 6.2%. Prabowo, speaking on Saturday, said he had instructed ministers to ensure the state receives at least “70% of the benefits from all mining permits” and added that, if necessary, the state should “take over stakes” in companies in Indonesia. The president did not spell out what constituted “benefits” or how the 70% would be calculated, leaving miners and analysts trying to assess whether he was referring to profits, revenue, taxes and royalties, or a broader measure of the state’s economic benefit. “We are still examining what President Prabowo meant by his intention for 70% of mining sector proceeds to go into state coffers,” Sudirman Widhy Hartono, chairman of the Association of Mining Professionals, told Reuters. He said the industry was awaiting a more detailed explanation from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources. The ministry did not respond to a request from Reuters for comment. A spokesperson for the president did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The mining sector, especially in nickel and coal, is already struggling with tighter production quotas and rising costs. French miner Eramet, which was forced to halt operations for several months due to a lower mining quota, is planning to sell some stake in its Indonesian nickel mine. “The mere uncertainty surrounding definitions is enough to delay new investment decisions,” said Fauzan Luthfi Djamal, mining analyst with brokerage Mirae Asset Sekuritas Indonesia. “Foreign partners involved in nickel downstreaming are likely re-evaluating project returns, while financing costs could potentially rise.” Mineral-rich Indonesia had seen massive investment in its nickel processing sector following a raw nickel export ban in 2020, and a similar ban on other minerals in 2023. Impact on companies Fauzan said the state’s objective of increasing revenue from natural resources is “understandable” but the challenge is designing a scheme that captures windfall gains without stifling business or deterring new investment. Sudirman said data from coal mining companies showed total state revenue can reach around 32% of total sales, while companies earn profits of less than 10% – which means government revenue is more than three times company profit. Depending on how the 70% “benefit” is calculated, Fauzan estimated net profits for privately owned miners could be cut by as much as half, while mines operating under special mining licences could see profits fall by up to a third. Fauzan said the quickest route would probably be through higher royalties, with the government having previously considered increases for gold, copper, silver, nickel and tin. Other possibilities include additional levies or requiring state equity participation when mining licences are extended or converted. Indonesia had earlier this year shelved plans to impose windfall taxes on coal and nickel exports and increase royalties on some mining companies. In May, Prabowo said exports of coal, palm oil and ferroalloys would be controlled by state-run Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia to combat exports being under-invoiced. The proposal was subsequently scaled back, with the agency saying its initial role would be as a centralised data collector. In August, Prabowo also announced a commodities exchange and said Indonesia should set its own prices rather than follow global benchmarks. “Prabowo often issues directives,” said Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, an economist at the Center of Economics and Law Studies think tank. “Yet the technical regulations are never prepared beforehand … we’re seeing this happen again.” (Reporting by Fransiska Nangoy and Bernadette Christina; Writing by Gibran Peshimam; Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan)
